narrative: The model estimated a 72.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, which is why your law school application was denied. This is a prediction, not a certainty, but it means the school treated your profile as high risk relative to applicants it admits. The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted-student average around the sixth decile. That academic signal weighed most heavily toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor; at 25.5 it was well below the accepted-student average of about 37.2, reinforcing the concern. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor. At 3.10 it was close to, though slightly below, the accepted average of 3.23, and among the top three factors it was the one that pushed toward passing rather than failure. Gender and race were not used in the decision. To move forward, ask admissions what evidence would best offset this prediction, and focus on a sustained record of stronger academic performance and a substantially improved LSAT if you reapply. Consider bar-exam preparation and academic advising early, and discuss with the school whether additional coursework or a revised application timeline could demonstrate readiness.
